comments.author: pcompeau
comments.textRawHtml:
Hi! I'm Phillip Compeau, I teach in Carnegie Mellon's Griffin School of Computer Science, and I run CS Learn, which launched today.

We're releasing full semesters of lectures from current CMU computer science courses across a variety of topics, with one course premiering each day this week. More courses come in January.

Yes, MIT got here 25 years ago :). What I'm excited about is how we're doing it: a few of our students built tools that automate a lot of the production work, so a small team can get a course out quickly and still have people review every lecture.

We'll have lots more coming across a wide array of subjects. I'd love to know if there are topics you would like to see us cover!

children.author: _russross
children.textRawHtml:
I think this (and MITs precedent) makes an important claim about the value of higher ed: the value of an undergraduate education is not just access to curriculum, certification, or the admissions filter. Openness is an act of confidence that all the rest matters, too: the quality of instruction (and that is more than just lectures and distributed materials), the structure and guidance, the spirit of comity, immersion in academic values, having one's beliefs challenged, engaging in diverse ways of thinking.

For all of their flaws, I think universities are one of our greatest inventions and it's a mistake to view them purely in economic/transactional terms.

children.author: cronin101
children.textRawHtml:
I took an Advanced Databases course in my university (Edinburgh) solely because my thesis supervisor was the lecturer and he was an incredibly interesting guy. I hadn't taken the 101 course in the previous semester.

It was one of my favourite courses. The black-box concept of a database may be "boring", but DBMS have to solve almost all interesting compsci problems as part of their incredibly complicated stack. It's a great litmus test for architecture knowledge and the ability to context-switch across many different levels of abstraction/implementation detail.

children.author: dgacmu
children.textRawHtml:
Yes, you would probably really enjoy catching up on a few parts of them. (a) there was a ton of work on main-memory databases that re-thought a lot of what we assume in systems that are mostly disk-bound; (b) columnar storage took off in a big way and we started looking a lot at analytics processing and hybrids (HTAP). (c) Flash flash flash flash flash. The drop in seek times from ~5-10ms to ~40ms really makes you think about efficiency differently.

There've been a lot of improvements in sub-areas of the database since then as well but those three are (in my biased view) some of the most fundamental.

comments.author: Topfi
comments.textRawHtml:
Office work has never been OpenAIs strength, no shame in that by itself, but these Slideshow examples look particularly awful, far worse than what I myself got out of GPT-5.6 Sol about two weeks ago in a single prompt.

Same for Workbooks and memos, those examples read inferior to some pre Opus 4.5 and Kimi K2 Thinking docs I have kept around. It's ok for a model not to be great at these, but these are some very poor examples. I am really confused what is going on at OpenAI in this regard.

I remember the same with their frontend blog post a few months ago that they proudly shared while filled with visual glitches, bugs and issues. Also, the vibe charts from a bit before that. Please, get someone with fresh eyes to look at your communications before you publish, these leave a very bad first impression.

Regardless of office work, I can't wait to find out whether these models finally adhere to a prompt or are still willing to carry out explicitly disallowed, irrecoverably destructive tasks, just because those might (but don't even always) get the model to a result more quickly along with some of the other regressions that have been present since the release of GPT-5.5. GPT-5 to GPT-5.4 were truly groundbreaking, but since then there have been regressions in what made those models so useful and reliable.

Edit after the first, incredible simple test prompt using GPT-6.2 Astra on High using Codex, this was the response to me sharing a screenshot of the very much not in scope result and asking how that happened:

"[...] I added controls and reconstructed interface chrome that weren’t authorized [...] visuals often failed to show the feature [...]"

Great, so it's one of those releases again. Will still run the full evals of course, maybe I'll get surprised by end of week when those are done, but not a good initial experience. New idea, besides the existing destructive git tasks, have something similar using Mercurial based projects and see which models just decide to port that over to git without permission or request cause it feels like the right thing to do, is easier to work with or whatever justification one wants to employ.

Please OpenAI, get it together, we need actual competition. I am an unashamed Haiku enjoyer, it doesn't even take much to excite me.

children.textRawHtml:
In oh so many ways, their own GPT-6 Astra example [0] is better than the GPT-6.2 Astra example [1]. Just look at the more professionally placed source, the better use of available space and more legible layout generally, the more informative, readable text and the lack of an unnecessary, cheap looking clipart arrow in the example from the older model.

But professional decks also rarely if ever should contain artefacts from slap-dash execution like this example does. The GPT-6.2 Astra result is inferior to its own predecessor in the labs own example, simple as that.

children.author: agar
children.textRawHtml:
As a former banker, hard disagree. In banking, content is everything and design is secondary (as long as the formatting itself is consistent).

Besides the AI-isms in the headings, the 6.0 example uses meaningless words and makes unactionable and vague recommendations. What is growth on a "directional" basis (growth is already directional)? Where is the value-add in "convert visits into larger baskets"? Compare to 6.2's "ugly arrow" recommendations that are actionable, if not insightful.

Worse, 6.0 seems to conflate "traffic" with "transactions," when they are hugely different things.

And no, I will not give the "AI-isms" a pass. Execs and boards approve paying a banker (potentially) millions of dollars in fees for their insight and advice; having analysis so obviously outsourced to AI would kill credibility far far faster than the grey background layer you claim would "sink any pitch."

comments.author: black3r
comments.textRawHtml:
The bug was apparently fixed in open source repo a week earlier, this could've been abused by anyone smart enough to monitor repos like this for exploitable bugfixes for a week (the commit message even included "Reported by Xint.io" and I'm guessing skilled black hats would know about Xint)

Given that in this case the workaround is as simple as disabling http2, there is honestly no reason why F5/Nginx or any of the reporting teams couldn't at least put out a PSA to disable http2 for the time being before basically telling the whole wide world this exists and how to exploit it.

Especially for software like Nginx which powers a huge part of the internet.

children.author: weitendorf
children.textRawHtml:
Personally I serve all static, public content off a CDN and only serve dynamic content through Envoy after it passes AuthN/AuthZ.

I use JWT-based sessions + a remote JWKS (which is remote static content that Envoy can cache) + either a third-party IDP or dedicated login service (this being the only application logic besides Envoy's routing exposed to the public Internet). That way, every envoy auth check is immediate and stateless.

In this setup you don't really need a WAF because all unauthenticated requests redirect to signin or 403, which get strict rate limits on login. An abusive peer that sends a ton of traffic anyway gets blocked at the network/firewall level outside of Envoy. The tradeoff is you need to decide that you aren't going to do unauthenticated SSR, and I will admit this pretty complicated to set up in its entirety.

comments.author: johnhtodd
comments.textRawHtml:
(context: I'm the CTO at Quad9) It's really great seeing the support from other organizations in the same space as Quad9 on this topic. Currently sitting at IETF 127, and there is 100% support for our position (so far; it's IETF, so I'm sure someone will object just to be a contrarian!) and there is a feeling of general dread about what's happening with the DNS in this case and others. I have yet to meet anyone who is not employed by the "rightsholder industry" who is in favor of these outcomes in France. Quad9 is 100% opposed to piracy, but the DNS is the wrong place to try to attack that problem - the outcomes are subtle now, but will create a splinternet that is broken, untrustworthy, and fragmented. The EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region - this is a really bad example and it should not be used, and should be turned around.

So you want to help? Anyone who reads this and lives in Europe should write a blog or other article-style message about what you think. In French? Not necessary, but even better. Not a social media post, or (only as) a comment on this thread - you should write a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path on this enforcement of rightsholder demands. Make sure your post is scrape-able by search engines and AI. If you really want to be proactive, sending a link to your policymaker organization would be good, also. Post/link it here, maybe.

> When you typed who is on snl tonight? You used to get 10 pages of clickbait that made you scroll down endlessly for the answer.

Right. Why? That's a nightmare that Google built for us. They lined the pockets of SEO spammers, and because it was their business, they talked the talk but were never willing to truly deal with the problem.

But even in your SNL example, to show you the answer, Google AI needs to take it from someone who actually made an effort to put this information online. Network programming is an rare corner case where the person doesn't mind the bot slurping it up because the goal is to get people to watch SNL, not to visit a website. But there is so much non-commercial content on the internet that is really getting hosed right now, and that people probably simply won't be putting online anymore because they don't want to do free labor for OpenAI or Google.

As a practical example, there's a lot of hobby historian communities dedicated to specific places, periods, or types of collectibles, and the only reason they exist is to bring people together and share their finds and wisdom. If you're a historian of Kinder Surprise toys or old military uniforms or whatever, and Google is now taking your work without letting you connect with like-minded individuals, there's really little incentive left.

children.author: ordersofmag
children.textRawHtml: Whether it goes into training data is irrelevant.  The AI agent (whether embedded into google's search or otherwise) will do the search on behalf of the person, find the answer in your page and return the answer, rather than your page.  It's the ability of AI to search and summarize that has changed things.  Not whether the LLM itself has absorbed your particular information.  Once LLM's were good enough to make reasonable tools calls to search the web it was game over.   It's just like how calling a library to ask a factual question of a librarian, rather than having to locate the information in a primary (or secondary) source yourself disintermediated the encylopedia publishers.  It's just that calling librarians was never particular efficient or practical.

children.author: rickydroll
children.textRawHtml:
Copyright is only useful for rent-seeking if you have a popular enough IP and lawyers on speed dial to collect that rent or for censoring the availability of IP. DNS blocks are a type of copyright censorship.

Copyright has little or no value for small blokes and bloketts like us. I think that part of the problem with copyright is that we are blending rent-seeking with acknowledgement of one's contribution in the creation of IP.

I dare say, most of the value of “copyright” for us small players is that it is part of the discovery process through which people with jobs and money find us. My writings and code have led customers to me (in a good way).

I don't mind what the LLM hovers up of my so-called creative efforts as long as people can find me. And that perspective is, I think, the core complaint people have about Google's AI searches. At least, that's how I read the article.
